newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey backs Cyprus talks, condemns arms build-up.
newsitem.headline: Turkey backs Cyprus talks, condemns arms build-up.

text.p: Turkey said on Tuesday it supported proposed face-to-face talks between Greek Cypriot and Turkish Cypriot leaders, but condemned Greek Cypriot military build-up on the divided island.

"Heavy armament being carried out by the Greek Cypriot side, the joint military doctrine between Greece and the Greek Cypriot administration...form a threat not only to the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, but to the security of Turkey and the region," a foreign ministry statement quoted by Anatolian news agency said.
But the United Nations-sponsored talks to be held in New York next week provided a suitable opportunity to reach a lasting settlement between the two communities in Cyprus, the statement added.
Cyprus president and Greek Cypriot leader Glafcos Clerides and Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash are due to meet for talks on July 9. It will be their first meeting for three years.
The Greek Cypriot government announced plans last year to buy Russian-made S-300 air defence missiles, scheduled for delivery in 1998. Ankara has threatened to use force if the missiles are deployed.
Earlier on Tuesday Greek Prime Minister Costas Simitis called on Turkey to withdraw its troops from northern Cyprus to help make the pending U.N.-sponsored talks successful.

Turkey has around 30,000 troops on the island, stationed there since 1974 when it invaded the northern third of the island in response to a Greek Cypriot coup backed by the military junta then ruling Greece.
The United Nations, which has had peacekeepers patrolling a tense "Green Line" dividing Cyprus since the mid-1970s, has been trying for years to reunite the island under a federal system.
Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Dentash said earlier on Tuesday he might pull out of the talks with Clerides if a document were put on the table before he had been informed of its contents.

But a U.N. source in New York responded by playing down the significance of the paper, saying it would be be largely a summary of remarks to be made by the U.N. special adviser for Cyprus, Diego Cordovez.
The source the intention would be to assist the two leaders by listing Cordovez's main talking points.
Greece and Turkey, although nominally allies within NATO, have often come close to war over the Cyprus problem and mineral and territorial rights in the Aegean Sea.
The self-declared Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, headed by Denktash, in the north of the island is recognised only by Turkey.
